title: The Wash-House and the Lasher: Kirriemuir, Kensington Gardens, and the Boy Who Would Not Grow Up
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kirriemuir, birth on Brechin Road
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a stone cottage on Brechin Road, among houses raised for the linen trade, a ninth child is born to David Barrie, handloom weaver, and Margaret Ogilvy. They name him James Matthew. The household is Calvinist, crowded, and poor in the way a weaving town is poor: the loom below, ten children above, scripture at the table and little else on it. The room he is born in can be crossed in three steps. It will be kept furnished and shown to visitors long after the last loom in Kirriemuir has stopped, the National Trust for Scotland holding the door.
suggested_refs: J. M. Barrie's Birthplace, 9 Brechin Road, Kirriemuir, in the care of the National Trust for Scotland
sources: National Trust for Scotland, Barrie's Birthplace
Nominatim, 9 Brechin Road DD8 4BX (coordinate correction from the published 56.6721/-3.0027)

stops.name: Kirriemuir, the wash-house theatre
stops.date_confidence: traditional: Barrie's own memoir places these theatricals in boyhood and gives no year; the date shown is a placeholder within the 1866-1870 span
stops.campa: Behind the cottage stands a small stone wash-house. The boy takes it, hangs a curtain across the door, and stages plays there for the children of the neighbourhood. He writes them himself and takes the admission at the door. His mother is the audience he is playing to, and she is the hardest of them to hold. Everything in the trade he will follow for fifty years is already in this outbuilding: a room persuaded to be another country, and a woman in the front row who has to be made to forget something.
stops.quote: For when you looked into my mother's eyes you knew, as if He had told you, why God sent her into the world, it was to open the minds of all who looked to beautiful thoughts.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Margaret Ogilvy (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The wash-house behind 9 Brechin Road, presented by the National Trust for Scotland as the site of Barrie's first plays
sources: National Trust for Scotland, Barrie's Birthplace

stops.name: Kirriemuir, the death of David
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the exact date is not established by any source reached, which give only 1867 and the phrase 'the day before his fourteenth birthday'
stops.campa: David Barrie, the mother's favourite, goes out on the ice and does not come home. He dies the day before his fourteenth birthday. James is six. He begins to wear his brother's clothes and to learn his brother's whistle, and goes into the darkened room to be taken, for a moment, for the dead boy. Margaret Ogilvy will not fully leave that room again. The son who survives will write for fifty years about a boy fixed at one age who cannot be aged past it. He never puts in print where that boy came from.
stops.quote: I thought it was the dead boy she was speaking to, and I said in a little lonely voice, 'No, it's no him, it's just me.'
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Margaret Ogilvy (1896), Chapter I, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Margaret Ogilvy (1896), Barrie's memoir of his mother and of his brother's death

stops.name: Glasgow, the Academy in Elmbank Street
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the coordinate is the Academy's original Elmbank Street site, since the school did not move to Colebrooke Street until 1878, ten years after Barrie's arrival
stops.campa: At about eight he is sent away from the house of grief to Glasgow, where his elder brother Alexander teaches and his sister Mary Ann keeps the household. The Academy stands in Elmbank Street, in a city of shipyards and soot, and what separates it from Kirriemuir is not the distance: nobody in this house is mourning. He is a small boy among older ones, boarded with his own family, schooled and removed from his mother's grief in the one move. The school will move house before he is twenty; he is here while it is still in its first building.
suggested_refs: The Glasgow Academy's original Elmbank Street building, occupied until the 1878 move to Colebrooke Street
sources: Nominatim and the Academy's own move history (correcting the published 55.8721/-4.2708, which points at the post-1878 site)

stops.name: Forfar, the year nearer home
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the coordinate resolves the modern Turfbeg campus, whereas the school Barrie attended in 1870 stood in the town centre
stops.campa: At about ten he is brought back within reach of Kirriemuir and put to Forfar Academy, five miles down the road, living again where his mother is. The interlude is short and leaves almost no trace in anything he wrote. It returns him to Angus at the age when a landscape sets, to the glens above the town and the shut Sunday streets. The towns in his books will carry other names and this geography. Within four years he is sent away again, and further.
suggested_refs: Forfar Academy, whose nineteenth-century building stood in the town centre, not on the present Turfbeg site
sources: Nominatim, Forfar Academy DD8 3TG (correcting the published 56.6428/-2.8901)

stops.name: Dumfries, the garden at Moat Brae
stops.date_confidence: the sources disagree by a year: the chronology gives enrolment at Dumfries Academy in 1874, the geography gives the Dumfries period as 1873-1878; both derive from the same article and the disagreement is not resolved here
stops.campa: At fourteen he is at Dumfries Academy, boarding with Alexander's family, reading Ballantyne and Fenimore Cooper past the hour, and writing plays to be acted by his friends. Behind a Georgian townhouse in George Street runs a sloping garden down toward the Nith, with trees to climb and walls to drop from. Here the pirates are invented. Decades later, in public, he names those games as the thing that became the play. He says that much about the source of almost nothing else he wrote.
stops.quote: When Shades of night began to fall certain young mathematicians shed their triangles and crept up trees and down walls in an odyssey which was long after to become the play of Peter Pan.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Moat Brae'
suggested_refs: Moat Brae, 101 George Street, Dumfries, which housed the National Centre for Children's Literature and Storytelling from June 2019 until its closure in August 2024

segments.name: Edinburgh, Nottingham, and the Trade of Letters

stops.name: Edinburgh, the degree taken against the family's wish
stops.date_confidence: attested for the conferral of the M.A.; the four years of study run from 1878
stops.campa: He reads literature at Edinburgh, which is not what a weaver's household wants of a clever son; they want the ministry. He reviews plays for the student press instead and takes his M.A. on the twenty-first of April 1882. The city has form for this: Adam Smith lectured here under Kames and was given its freedom, and Alexander Graham Bell was born a mile away and left, like Barrie, for London and then further. Barrie will come back to this quadrangle almost fifty years later with a chancellor's title, and not before.
suggested_refs: The University of Edinburgh matriculation and graduation registers, session 1878-1882
sources: Edinburgh pin inherited byte-identical from adam_smith.journey.json

stops.name: Nottingham, a year and a half of leaders
stops.date_confidence: the engagement is attested as roughly eighteen months beginning after his 1882 graduation; no start date is recorded
stops.campa: No Edinburgh paper will take him, so he goes south to a staff post on the Nottingham Journal and writes leaders for about a year and a half. It is the only regular salary of his life. It teaches him the short sentence that has to land in a column an inch wide, and the paragraph that cannot afford a second try. His prose keeps both for fifty years. Then the engagement ends. The paper does not fold, whatever is said later; it goes on for another seventy years without him.
suggested_refs: Barrie's unsigned leaders in the Nottingham Journal, 1883-1884
sources: negative check against the Nottingham Journal's own publication history, which continues into the 1950s

stops.name: Kirriemuir, the return and the mother's stories
stops.date_confidence: attested as the year his sketches begin appearing in the St James's Gazette
stops.campa: Out of work, he comes home to his parents' house and starts sending sketches of small-town Scottish life to the St James's Gazette in London. The material is not his. It is his mother's: her recollections of Kirriemuir before the power looms, the Auld Licht congregations, the weavers' funerals, told across a kitchen and taken down by a son who has been listening to her since he was six and trying to hold her attention. He sells the town he was born in, by the column, to an English paper, and it works.
stops.quote: She lived twenty-nine years after his death, such active years, until toward the end, that you never knew where she was unless you took hold of her.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Margaret Ogilvy (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Barrie's St James's Gazette sketches, 1884 onward, the raw material of the Thrums books

stops.name: London, arrival with a portfolio of Scottish sketches
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: He comes to London in 1885 to live by his pen, with nothing behind him but a folder of Angus sketches and the addresses of two editors. He spends the days in the reading room and on the walk to Fleet Street, waiting on editors who have not answered. Arthur Edward Waite is working the same city in the same decade, moving between Theosophy in Holland Park and the Golden Dawn and the Rosicrucians in the City; the two men never meet on any page that survives. London in the eighties is large enough to hold a magician and a Scotch journalist a mile apart and introduce neither.
suggested_refs: The British Museum Reading Room, working address of London's freelance journalists in the 1880s
sources: London pin inherited byte-identical from arthur_edward_waite.journey.json and maurice_sendak.journey.json

stops.name: The British Museum Reading Room, the Thrums books
stops.date_confidence: attested: Auld Licht Idylls 1888, A Window in Thrums 1889, The Little Minister 1891
stops.campa: Auld Licht Idylls appears in 1888, A Window in Thrums in 1889, The Little Minister in 1891. Kirriemuir, renamed Thrums, becomes a place the English reading public believes it knows. Sentimental and exact and salable, the books make him. They also fix him as a regional writer, a Scotchman with a district. Within four years he is writing for the stage instead. The material was his mother's; the reputation is his; the town gets neither, and gets tourists.
stops.quote: From the day on which I first tasted blood in the garret my mind was made up; there could be no hum-dreadful-drum profession for me; literature was my game.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Margaret Ogilvy (1896), Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Auld Licht Idylls (1888) and A Window in Thrums (1889), first editions

stops.name: Toole's Theatre, William IV Street: the first plays
stops.date_confidence: the pool carried a contradiction: it dated Walker, London to 1891 and called it his first London play. Wikipedia gives Ibsen's Ghost, or Toole Up-to-Date as the first, 1891, and Walker, London as his third, opened 1892 for 497 performances. This stop follows Wikipedia and leaves the disagreement standing
stops.campa: At J. L. Toole's small house near Charing Cross, Barrie gets onto the London stage with Ibsen's Ghost, a burlesque, in 1891. The following year Walker, London runs there for four hundred and ninety-seven performances and settles the question of whether the Thrums man can write dialogue. In its company is a young actress named Mary Ansell. He is thirty-two, four feet eleven or thereabouts, and has just discovered that a theatre will do in an evening what a novel takes a year to do. He does not go back to being only a novelist.
suggested_refs: Toole's Theatre, William IV Street, Westminster, demolished 1896 for the Charing Cross Hospital extension

stops.name: Vailima, Samoa: the invitation not taken
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the correspondence and the invitation are biographical tradition and were not verified against any letter this session; the date is a placeholder inside Stevenson's Samoan years, 1890-1894
stops.campa: Robert Louis Stevenson, another Scot who went south and did not stop, writes from a house he has built on a hill above Apia and asks Barrie to come. Barrie does not come. He will not cross an ocean for anyone, and there is no record that he ever seriously tried. Stevenson dies at Vailima in 1894 and the two never see each other. The man who will invent an island reachable only by flying turns down the one real island he is asked to. His geography keeps the hole where the Pacific would have been.
stops.quote: The artistic callings--you remember how Stevenson thumped them--are merely doing what you are clamorous to be at; it is not real work unless you would rather be doing something else.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, 'Courage', Rectorial Address, University of St Andrews, 3 May 1922, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Barrie-Stevenson correspondence, cited in biographical tradition but not located in a published edition this session
sources: biographical tradition regarding the Barrie-Stevenson letters, not independently verified
J. M. Barrie, 'Courage' (1922), for the quotation

stops.name: Kirriemuir, the marriage to Mary Ansell
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He marries the actress in his own town on the ninth of July 1894, having nearly died of pneumonia first and been nursed by her through it. There are no children. Biographers report the marriage was never consummated, which is a claim about a bedroom made by people who were not in it and is repeated here as report, not as fact. What is not in dispute is that the couple keep a Saint Bernard called Porthos, and that the dog, not the wife, is the reason Barrie is in Kensington Gardens every afternoon within three years.
stops.quote: I don't believe that Uncle Jim ever experienced what one might call 'a stirring in the undergrowth' for anyone, man, woman, or child.
stops.quote_source: Nico Llewelyn Davies, quoted in Andrew Birkin, J.M. Barrie and the Lost Boys, as cited in Wikipedia, 'J. M. Barrie'
suggested_refs: The 1894 marriage register of Kirriemuir parish
sources: Birkin, J.M. Barrie and the Lost Boys, quoted at second hand and not consulted directly

stops.name: Gloucester Road, the house in Kensington
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of purchase
stops.campa: The Barries buy a house on Gloucester Road, a respectable address for a successful man of letters, and set up the arrangement that will hold for fourteen years and then break: a wife with a career she gives up, a husband at his desk, a garden, a dog, no children. Sentimental Tommy comes out in 1896 and Margaret Ogilvy in the same year, a memoir of his mother, of her grief for David, and of the six-year-old who put on the dead boy's clothes to be mistaken for him. He publishes nothing about her afterwards.
suggested_refs: Margaret Ogilvy (1896) and Sentimental Tommy (1896), the two books of the Gloucester Road years

segments.name: Kensington Gardens and the Boy Castaways

stops.name: Kensington Gardens, the meeting by the Long Water
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Walking Porthos along the Long Water he falls in with two small boys in red tam-o'-shanters, George and Jack Llewelyn Davies, and their nurse. Their mother is Sylvia, daughter of George du Maurier; their father Arthur is a barrister who will never much like him. From this afternoon everything else in Barrie's life is downstream. He returns to these same gardens, and to this same family, summer after summer in the years that follow, and the boy who will not grow up is being assembled here out of real children, long before he has a name.
stops.quote: Two is the beginning of the end.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 1, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Long Water and the Broad Walk, Kensington Gardens, Barrie's daily walk from 1897
sources: hans_christian_andersen.journey.json and james_joyce.journey.json, which pin Kensington at 51.5015/-0.1875, a point deliberately kept distinct from this one

stops.name: 100 Bayswater Road, rooms above the Gardens
stops.date_confidence: attested from about 1900; the tenancy runs to about 1909, not to 1902 as an earlier draft had it
stops.campa: He takes rooms on the north side of the park, so that the Gardens and the games in them are in view from the desk. Here he writes The Little White Bird, a novel for adults, and buries inside it the chapters in which a boy named Peter Pan appears in print for the first time, flying out of a nursery window at seven days old to live among the birds on the island in the Serpentine. The Admirable Crichton is staged the same year. One of the two is the better play, and it is not the one anybody remembers.
suggested_refs: The Little White Bird (1902), whose central chapters were reissued as Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens

stops.name: Black Lake Cottage, Tilford: the castaways photographed
stops.date_confidence: the lease runs from about 1900 to about 1907; the Boy Castaways album is made in the summer of 1901
stops.campa: On heathland near Farnham he leases a cottage with a black lake in front of it, and the Davies boys are brought down for weekends of cricket, amateur theatricals, and marooning. He photographs them in the character of shipwrecked castaways and has the results privately printed and bound as The Boy Castaways of Black Lake Island, with himself credited as the boys' captain. Two copies are made. Arthur Llewelyn Davies leaves his on a train. The book is the play before the play, and the boys are already in costume.
stops.quote: He was an innocent, which is why he could write Peter Pan.
stops.quote_source: Nico Llewelyn Davies, quoted in Andrew Birkin, J.M. Barrie and the Lost Boys, as cited in Wikipedia, 'J. M. Barrie'
suggested_refs: The Boy Castaways of Black Lake Island (1901), privately printed in two copies

stops.name: Egerton House, Berkhamsted: the family and the father
stops.date_confidence: the family's residence 1904-1907 is attested; Arthur Llewelyn Davies dies in 1907
stops.campa: The Llewelyn Davieses move out to an Elizabethan house in Hertfordshire and Barrie follows them there, constantly, a small famous man arriving with presents. Arthur endures him. In 1906 a growth is found in Arthur's jaw and the surgery takes half his face; Barrie pays, writes down what the dying man says, and is present at the end in 1907. Sylvia and the five boys come back to London. What the family had tolerated as an eccentricity is now the household's working arrangement.
suggested_refs: Egerton House, Berkhamsted, demolished 1937; the Llewelyn Davies residence 1904-1907

stops.name: Duke of York's Theatre, the premiere
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Peter Pan, or The Boy Who Wouldn't Grow Up opens in St Martin's Lane two days after Christmas, with Nina Boucicault as the first Peter and a stagehand's whistle for Tinker Bell. The audience is asked to save a life by clapping and does. Shaw calls it ostensibly a holiday entertainment for children but really a play for grown-up people, and the phrase survives at second hand, without a text behind it. The play is revived every Christmas in London for decades; Barrie keeps rewriting it and does not publish a script for twenty-four years.
stops.quote: Second to the right, and then straight on till morning.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 3, 'Come Away, Come Away!', Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Duke of York's Theatre, St Martin's Lane, and the 1904 promptbook of Peter Pan
sources: the Shaw phrase is carried at second hand from Wikipedia's own prose; no primary Shaw text was located

stops.name: Empire Theatre, New York: Peter Pan on Broadway
stops.date_confidence: the source reached states only that a Broadway production was mounted in 1905 at the Empire with Maude Adams; the exact date is reconstruction, and no source establishes that Barrie crossed the Atlantic for it
stops.campa: Maude Adams plays Peter at the Empire, on Broadway at Fortieth Street, and America takes the part as hers for a generation; she will play it more than fifteen hundred times. The play becomes an American Christmas institution in parallel with the English one, on a continent its author is not standing on. Barrie is a notoriously reluctant traveller and nothing places him in the house. The boy who could not be got to grow up crosses the ocean; the man who wrote him stays in London.
suggested_refs: The Empire Theatre, 1430 Broadway at 40th Street, demolished 1953
sources: coordinate corrected to the Empire's actual address from the published 40.759/-73.9885

stops.name: 3 Adelphi Terrace, the divorce and the flat above the river
stops.date_confidence: the divorce is attested to October 1909; the move to Adelphi Terrace follows it, and the flat is held until his death
stops.campa: Mary Ansell has been having an affair with the writer Gilbert Cannan, seventeen years her junior. Barrie offers her the choice, she takes Cannan, and the divorce goes through in October. He gives up the house and takes a flat on Adelphi Terrace looking over the Thames, third floor and then, from 1917, fourth. He keeps it twenty-eight years. Friends note the enormous fireplace and the absence of anything domestic. He has lost a wife and is about to be handed five children.
suggested_refs: 3 Adelphi Terrace, Barrie's London address 1909-1937

stops.name: London, the death of Sylvia and the guardianship
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the precise legal and practical arrangements are described differently across accounts and are not settled here
stops.campa: Three years after Arthur, Sylvia dies of cancer, and the five brothers are orphaned. Barrie takes them on, alongside their nurse Mary Hodgson, and pays for everything from Eton onward. What exactly he was given, and by whom, and whether Sylvia's written wishes said what he later said they said, is told differently by every account, and no version reached here settles it. He is fifty, childless, recently divorced, and now, by some instrument nobody can produce cleanly, the guardian of five boys.
suggested_refs: Sylvia Llewelyn Davies's will and the disputed transcription of her wishes
sources: London pin inherited byte-identical from maurice_sendak.journey.json

stops.name: London, Peter and Wendy in prose
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication
stops.campa: Seven years after the play, Barrie writes the story down as a novel and it acquires the sentences everyone quotes. The prose is stranger than the stage version, harder, and much colder about mothers: the window is shut, the beds are given away, the boy at the pane finds he has been replaced. He writes it in the Adelphi flat, guardian of five living boys, with the eldest at Cambridge and the youngest eight. It is the last full-length thing he writes about children while none of them is dead.
stops.quote: All children, except one, grow up. They soon know that they will grow up, and the way Wendy knew was this.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 1, 'Peter Breaks Through', Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Peter and Wendy (1911), Hodder and Stoughton, first edition
sources: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Wikisource

stops.name: The Ross Ice Shelf, the last letter from the tent
stops.date_confidence: Scott's party reached its final camp on 19 March 1912 and the letters are undated; the coordinate is the conventional placement of that camp, roughly twelve and a half miles short of One Ton Depot, and is not a surveyed point
stops.campa: Eleven thousand miles away, in a tent that will not be opened for eight months, Robert Falcon Scott writes to seven people. One of them is Barrie, godfather to Scott's son Peter, and the letter asks him to look after the family and defends the expedition. Barrie carries it in his pocket for the rest of his life and reads from it at St Andrews ten years later. That he also wrote the introduction to Scott's Last Expedition is repeated everywhere and is not supported by the 1913 edition, whose introduction is by Sir Clements Markham.
suggested_refs: Scott's letter to Barrie, March 1912, quoted in the rectorial address 'Courage' (1922)
sources: the claim of a Barrie introduction to Scott's Last Expedition is flagged as unverified

stops.name: Kensington Gardens, the statue put up in the night
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Without permit and without announcement, George Frampton's bronze is carried into the Gardens overnight and stands there on May Morning, so that children walking out will believe fairies brought it. The Times prints a notice Barrie paid for. He is disappointed with it: it doesn't show the devil in Peter, he says. Frampton had meant to work from photographs of Michael Llewelyn Davies in the costume and used another child instead. The statue is listed Grade II* in 1970 and copied six times for parks across the Empire.
suggested_refs: Sir George Frampton's Peter Pan, Kensington Gardens, unveiled 30 April 1912, Grade II* listed 1970

stops.name: London, created a baronet
stops.date_confidence: the creation is attested to 14 June 1913; the ceremonial detail at court is reconstruction
stops.campa: George V makes him a baronet. He is Sir James Matthew Barrie, and the title is hereditary, which is a joke nobody makes out loud: he has no children and the baronetcy will die with him in twenty-four years. The weaver's ninth child has a coat of arms. Kirriemuir reads it in the papers. In eighteen months the eldest of the five boys he is raising will be in a trench in Flanders, and the honours of 1913 will begin to look like the last quiet year anybody had.
suggested_refs: The London Gazette entry creating the Barrie baronetcy, June 1913

stops.name: St Eloi, near Ypres: George killed
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: George Llewelyn Davies, the boy in the red tam-o'-shanter from the Long Water, twenty-one, an officer of the King's Royal Rifle Corps, is shot by a sniper at St Eloi while resting during a briefing before an advance. Barrie had written to him three days earlier that he was in the pit of despair about him. The eldest of the five is the first to go. Barrie learns of it in London, at fifty-four, five years into the guardianship, and has four boys left of the five he was given.
suggested_refs: The St Eloi sector of the Ypres Salient, March 1915

stops.name: Voormezeele Enclosure No. 3, the reburial
stops.date_confidence: the first burial near where he fell and the later removal to this cemetery are both attested; the date of the removal is not established by any source reached, so the stop carries the date of his death
stops.campa: He is buried first near where he fell and moved afterwards to a Commonwealth war cemetery outside Voormezele, where the headstone stands among thousands from the Salient in rows that make no distinction between a rifleman and the boy who was the original of Peter Pan. Barrie never goes. The grave is four hours from London and he does not make the crossing, as he did not cross to New York and did not cross to Samoa. He mourns at a desk, which is where he does everything.
suggested_refs: Voormezeele Enclosure No. 3, Commonwealth War Graves Commission, Ieper
sources: Nominatim, Voormezeele Enclosure No. 3 (correcting the published 50.8067/2.8697)

stops.name: St Andrews, elected Rector
stops.date_confidence: the three-year term beginning 1919 is attested; the election date is not recorded here
stops.campa: The students of St Andrews elect him Rector for three years. It is a students' office, given by their vote and not by any faculty, and he takes it seriously enough to spend three years failing to write the address he owes them. He is fifty-nine. Two of the five boys are dead or about to be. He is the most successful playwright in the English-speaking world and cannot get a sentence down about what he has learned, and will not manage it until the third year of the term.
stops.quote: You shall cut it, so it is ordained, every one of you for himself, and its name is Courage.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, 'Courage', Rectorial Address, University of St Andrews, 3 May 1922, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The Rectorship of the University of St Andrews, 1919-1922

stops.name: Sandford Lasher, near Oxford: Michael drowns
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Michael Llewelyn Davies, an Oxford undergraduate a month short of twenty-one, the boy Barrie loved best and the one Frampton was to have modelled the statue on, drowns in the pool below the weir at Sandford with his friend Rupert Buxton. The coroner finds Davies drowned accidentally and Buxton drowned trying to save him. Others in the family said afterwards it was a pact. Both accounts are in the record and neither dislodges the other. Michael could not swim. He was learning that spring.
stops.quote: To die will be an awfully big adventure.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 8, 'The Mermaids' Lagoon', Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: Sandford Lasher, the pool below Sandford Lock on the Thames, and the 1921 coroner's inquest
sources: Nominatim, Sandford Lock OX4 4YB (correcting the published 51.7011/-1.2273)

stops.name: St John-at-Hampstead churchyard, the grave of Michael
stops.date_confidence: the burial here is attested; the date of the funeral is not established by the sources reached, so the stop carries the date of the drowning
stops.campa: He is buried on the hill at Hampstead. Barrie called him the boy who made me, and after this stops writing plays that matter. Nico, the youngest, said later that his guardian never recovered and never pretended to. Two of five are in the ground now, one under Flanders clay and one under a London churchyard, and the man who is supposed to be their father in all but law is sixty-one and has a bronze statue of a boy who cannot die standing three miles south of this grave.
suggested_refs: The churchyard of St John-at-Hampstead, burial place of Michael Llewelyn Davies

stops.name: St Andrews, the address on courage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A year after Sandford he stands up in front of the students and delivers the address he owes them. He reads from the letter Scott wrote in the tent. He talks about ambition, about failure, about the dead of the war whose places these young men are sitting in, and about the one virtue he says is the only one that carries the others. He is sixty-one, speaking to strangers in a hall in Fife, and neither of his dead boys is named anywhere in the hour.
stops.quote: Courage is the thing. All goes if courage goes.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, 'Courage', Rectorial Address, University of St Andrews, 3 May 1922, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: 'Courage', the rectorial address of 3 May 1922, published the same year

segments.name: Chancellor, Copyright, and the Freedom of the Town

stops.name: London, the Order of Merit
stops.date_confidence: attested to the New Year Honours of January 1922; no day is recorded
stops.campa: In the New Year Honours he is appointed to the Order of Merit, which is in the sovereign's personal gift, limited to twenty-four living holders, and cannot be bought or lobbied for. It is the highest civil distinction available to a British writer. He receives it four months before he stands up at St Andrews to tell a hall of students that everything goes if courage goes. The medal and the address belong to the same year, and only one of them is still read.
suggested_refs: The New Year Honours list, January 1922

stops.name: University College Dundee, opening the playing fields
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the day of the visit is not recorded
stops.campa: He comes to Dundee with Field Marshal Earl Haig to open the college's new playing fields. Haig commanded the armies in which George Llewelyn Davies was killed at St Eloi seven years before, and the two men cut a ribbon on a cricket ground twenty miles from Kirriemuir. Barrie founded his own cricket club in the nineties, the Allahakbarries, whose members could mostly not play and included Conan Doyle and Wodehouse. Games are the one register in which he never wrote anything sad.
suggested_refs: The 1922 opening of University College Dundee's playing fields by Barrie and Earl Haig

stops.name: Eilean Shona, Loch Moidart
stops.date_confidence: the lease and the summers there are attested to the 1920s; the year given is that of the Peter Pan screenplay written on the island
stops.campa: He leases a tidal island in Loch Moidart, on the west Highland coast, and takes Nico there for the summers. On it he writes the screenplay for the silent Peter Pan of 1924 and most of A Kiss for Cinderella. The island is small and wooded, cut off twice a day by the tide and reachable only by boat. For those summers he is living inside a piece of his own scenery. Readers have held ever since that Eilean Shona is the island of Mary Rose, the play about a girl who vanishes and comes back unaged.
suggested_refs: Eilean Shona, Loch Moidart, and the 1924 Paramount silent film of Peter Pan
sources: the identification with Mary Rose is a traditional reading, not a documented statement by Barrie

stops.name: Bowring Park, St John's: the boy in bronze for a drowned child
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Frampton casts six more of the Kensington statue for parks around the Empire and Europe. The Newfoundland one is unveiled in Bowring Park as a memorial to Betty Munn, a child drowned in the sinking of the SS Florizel in February 1918. Brussels gets one in 1924, shot through with bullets in the next war; Liverpool, Perth, Toronto, and Camden in New Jersey follow by 1929. A figure invented so that a boy would not have to die is set up, six times over, on top of children who did.
suggested_refs: The Peter Pan statue in Bowring Park, St John's, unveiled 29 August 1925 in memory of Betty Munn

stops.name: Great Ormond Street, the copyright given away
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1929; no day is recorded
stops.campa: In April 1929 Barrie assigns the copyright of everything Peter Pan, the play, Peter and Wendy, Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens, and The Little White Bird, to the children's hospital in Bloomsbury, and asks that the income never be disclosed. It is not disclosed to this day. He is sixty-eight, has no heirs, and gives the most valuable property in English children's literature to a building full of sick children a mile from the Gardens where he met the boys.
suggested_refs: The 1929 deed of gift of the Peter Pan copyright to Great Ormond Street Hospital for Children

stops.name: Edinburgh, Chancellor of the University
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of election; he holds the office until his death in 1937
stops.campa: Forty-eight years after taking his M.A. in this quadrangle against his family's wishes, he is elected Chancellor of the University of Edinburgh, and holds the office until he dies. It is the ceremonial head of the institution that would have made him a minister. He confers degrees in the hall where he was conferred one, an old man in a gold-trimmed gown who came here on a weaver's savings and reviewed plays for the student paper because nobody else would print him.
suggested_refs: Old College, University of Edinburgh, seat of the Chancellorship

stops.name: Kirriemuir Town Hall, the Freedom of the burgh
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the seventh of June the burgh gives him its Freedom in the town hall, three hundred yards from the cottage where he was born and half a mile from the ground he will be buried in. He is seventy. He has spent forty-five years selling this town to England under the name of Thrums, and the town, which has been variously flattered and annoyed by it, votes him the highest thing it has to give. Both the cottage and the grave are within a ten-minute walk of the room he stands up in.
suggested_refs: The burgess roll of Kirriemuir, 7 June 1930
sources: Nominatim, Kirriemuir Town Hall DD8 4BS (correcting the published 56.6717/-3.0022)

segments.name: The Grave and What Outlives It

stops.name: Manchester Street, Marylebone: death in a nursing home
stops.date_confidence: attested; how long before the nineteenth he was moved here from the Adelphi Terrace flat, which he had kept since 1909, is not reconciled by any source reached
stops.campa: He dies of pneumonia on the nineteenth of June, seventy-seven years old, in a nursing home off Manchester Square. The estate goes almost entirely to his secretary, Lady Cynthia Asquith, with the rights to all the Peter Pan works excluded, because those were given away eight years before and are not his to leave. Of the five brothers, Peter, Jack, and Nico are alive. The baronetcy created in 1913 dies with him, as everyone knew it would when it was made.
suggested_refs: Barrie's will, leaving the residue to Lady Cynthia Asquith but excluding the Peter Pan rights

stops.name: Kirriemuir Cemetery, the grave beside his parents
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is brought north and buried at Kirriemuir beside David Barrie, Margaret Ogilvy, and two of his brothers and sisters, in the ground of the town he left at eighteen and never stopped writing. The story that he declined Westminster Abbey is repeated everywhere and is not in any source reached here; it is carried as tradition and no further. What is certain is the arrangement of the stones. The weaver, the mother, the boy who drowned under the ice at thirteen, and the man who made him immortal, in one plot.
suggested_refs: The Barrie family plot, Kirriemuir Cemetery, Northmuir
sources: Nominatim, Kirriemuir Cemetery (correcting two conflicting published values, 56.665/-3.0075 and 56.6739/-3.0117)

stops.name: Kirriemuir, 9 Brechin Road: the cottage kept open
stops.date_confidence: the National Trust for Scotland's ownership of the birthplace is attested; the date of acquisition is not established by any source reached, so the stop carries the date of the burial as a placeholder and makes no claim about when the museum opened
stops.campa: The cottage on Brechin Road is kept as it was and opened to visitors, the wash-house behind it labelled as the first theatre. Children are brought through a weaver's room the size of a boat, in a town of nine thousand people in Angus, to look at the place where the story started. Half a mile off is the plot with four Barries in it. The house and the grave are within one walk of each other. The boy who could not be got to grow up is in neither: he stands in bronze in Kensington Gardens and belongs, on paper, to a hospital in Bloomsbury.
stops.quote: When Margaret grows up she will have a daughter, who is to be Peter's mother in turn; and so it will go on, so long as children are gay and innocent and heartless.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 17, closing lines, Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: J. M. Barrie's Birthplace, National Trust for Scotland
sources: National Trust for Scotland, Barrie's Birthplace

stops.name: London, Sloane Square: the last of the Peter Pan boys but one
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 April 1960 at Sloane Square Underground station; no verified coordinate for the station was obtained, so the atlas's canonical London pin is used in its place
stops.campa: Peter Llewelyn Davies, publisher, sixty-three, who spent his adult life being introduced as the real Peter Pan and called the book that terrible masterpiece, throws himself under a train arriving at Sloane Square. The coroner's jury finds that he killed himself while the balance of his mind was disturbed. He is not the last of the five: Nico, the youngest, who always said he was the only one the story never touched, lives another twenty years and dies in 1980.
stops.quote: Because they are no longer gay and innocent and heartless. It is only the gay and innocent and heartless who can fly.
stops.quote_source: J. M. Barrie, Peter and Wendy (1911), Chapter 17, 'When Wendy Grew Up', Wikisource edition
suggested_refs: The April 1960 inquest into the death of Peter Llewelyn Davies
sources: London pin inherited byte-identical from the atlas canon

stops.name: Great Ormond Street, the right that does not expire
stops.date_confidence: attested: UK copyright expired in 1987, the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act granting the perpetual royalty right received Royal Assent in 1988, the EU term extension restored full copyright in 1996, and that term lapsed again in 2007
stops.campa: Fifty years after Barrie's death the copyright expires, and Parliament writes the hospital a clause of its own: a perpetual right to royalties on any public performance or publication of Peter Pan in the United Kingdom. Commentators note it is the only thing of its kind in British law apart from the King James Bible. The European term extension of 1996 hands the hospital full copyright again until 2007, after which the perpetual clause resumes alone. An authorised sequel, Peter Pan in Scarlet, follows in 2006.
suggested_refs: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, Schedule 6; Geraldine McCaughrean, Peter Pan in Scarlet (2006)
